plan.chapterName: OpenStax Organic Chemistry, chapter 5: Stereochemistry at Tetrahedral Centers
plan.contextChunk: This figure arranges three generalized carbon compounds in three rows and reflects each one in a drawn mirror. Each row begins at the left with a condensed formula written in colored letters, "CH3X", "CH2XY", and "CHXYZ", with X in magenta, Y in blue, and Z in gold. Next comes a structural drawing in which a central "C" bonds upward by a plain line, to the left and right by plain lines, and downward by a heavy wedge; the four attached labels are X, H, H and H in the top row, X, H, Y and H in the middle row, and X, H, Y and Z in the bottom row. Third in each row is a ball-and-stick model with a dark gray carbon carrying a red sphere above and green, blue, or yellow spheres below according to the substituents named. At the right stands a tall pale blue rectangular pane with a highlight streak, representing a mirror, and behind it each model appears again as its reflection, with the substituent spheres reversed left to right. Repeating the same three columns down every row isolates substitution pattern as the only variable, so the reader can test each reflection against its original. The layout introduces the condition under which a tetrahedral carbon and its mirror image cease to be superimposable, the structural basis of molecular handedness.

elements: Left column: condensed formula label for the active row — 'CH3X' (X magenta), 'CH2XY' (X magenta, Y blue), or 'CHXYZ' (X magenta, Y blue, Z gold), with 'C','H' in black/green
Second column: flat 2D structural drawing — central black 'C', plain line up to X, plain lines down-left to H and down-right to H or Y, bold solid wedge down to H or Z
Third column: 3D ball-and-stick original model — dark gray carbon sphere at center
Red substituent sphere (X) bonded upward from carbon
Green substituent spheres (H) bonded to lower-left / lower-right / front
Blue substituent sphere (Y) replacing one green H in rows 2 and 3
Yellow substituent sphere (Z) replacing a second green H in row 3
Gray cylindrical bonds from carbon to each substituent (tetrahedral, 109.5°)
Tall pale-blue translucent rectangular mirror pane standing vertically at the right, with a diagonal white highlight streak and a darker blue edge line on its right side
Mirror-image ball-and-stick model behind/inside the pane, left-right reversed relative to the original, rendered slightly desaturated as if seen through glass
Faint specular reflection glints on spheres

interactions.teaches: Only the variety of substituents changes across rows; with four different groups on tetrahedral carbon the mirror image becomes non-superimposable
interactions.label: Compound

interactions.teaches: Dragging and spinning the reflected model onto the original shows CH3X and CH2XY can be brought into coincidence, while CHXYZ always leaves two colored substituents swapped
Seeing the tetrahedral arrangement from other angles proves the mismatch in CHXYZ is real 3D handedness, not an artifact of one viewpoint
The formal test for chirality: bring the mirror image out of the pane, attempt best-fit alignment, and read whether every sphere color matches
interactions.label: Superimposition test

demo_steps.title: CH3X in the mirror
demo_steps.narration: One red X and three identical green H's on a tetrahedral carbon; the pale pane shows the reflection with left and right substituents exchanged.

demo_steps.title: CH3X superimposes
demo_steps.narration: Pull the reflection out and rotate it onto the original: because the three green H's are interchangeable, every sphere matches. The molecule is achiral.

demo_steps.title: CH2XY still superimposes
demo_steps.narration: With red X, blue Y and two green H's, a simple rotation about the C–X bond still brings the mirror image into full coincidence — two identical groups are enough to kill handedness.

demo_steps.title: CHXYZ fails the test
demo_steps.narration: Four different groups: no matter how the reflection is rotated, the blue and yellow spheres end up swapped. The two forms are non-superimposable mirror images — the carbon is a chirality center.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World units: carbon sphere radius 0.42 at origin of the model; substituent spheres radius 0.38; bond cylinders radius 0.09, bond length 1.25 (center-to-center), perfect tetrahedral directions — X up at (0, 1.25, 0); the other three at 109.5° from it: lower-left (-1.02, -0.42, -0.35), lower-right (+1.02, -0.42, -0.35), front-down (0, -0.42, +1.10) which is the bold-wedge position pointing toward the viewer. Original model sits at x = 0; mirror plane is a vertical plane with normal along +X at x = +2.6, so the reflected copy is centered at x = +5.2 with all x-coordinates negated (left-right reversal). Mirror pane: 3.2 wide (along Z, receding) × 6.0 tall (Y) × 0.08 thick, standing vertically, its face nearly parallel to the screen and tilted ~8° so the highlight streak reads; pale blue #cfe3f0 at ~0.35 opacity, right edge line #4a8cb5, one diagonal white streak at ~60° from lower-left to upper-right at 0.5 opacity. Left of the models, on the same horizontal band: condensed formula text at x = -6.5 (C and H black #1a1a1a with H subscript green #00a14b in the source, X magenta #e5007e, Y blue #0077c8, Z gold #b8860b), and the flat 2D structural drawing centered at x = -3.4 drawn in the XY plane facing the camera (black 'C', thin black lines up/left/right, filled black triangular wedge pointing down-front, label letters colored as above, H labels green). Sphere colors: carbon #4a4a4a (dark gray, specular), X red #b0392b, H green #45a545, Y blue #2aa3dd, Z yellow #d6c92e; mirrored copy uses the same hues at ~80% saturation to suggest glass. Row identity only changes which of the three non-X positions carry green/blue/yellow: CH3X = green, green, green; CH2XY = green(lower-left), blue(lower-right), green(front-wedge); CHXYZ = green(lower-left), blue(lower-right), yellow(front-wedge). Whole scene spans about x ∈ [-7.5, 7], y ∈ [-3.2, 3.2].
interactionPlan.notes: Build one reusable molecule group (carbon + 4 substituents + bonds) and instantiate it twice; generate the mirror copy with scale(-1,1,1) on a parent group so it is a true reflection, then compensate geometry normals (THREE.Mesh material side = DoubleSide, or negate normals) to avoid inverted lighting. Mirror pane: MeshPhysicalMaterial, transmission ~0.6, roughness 0.15, transparent, depthWrite false, rendered last for correct blending; the streak is an additive plane or a canvas-texture gradient. Drag: raycast onto a plane parallel to the camera for translation; drag with modifier / horizontal drag beyond a threshold applies trackball rotation to the mirror copy only. Superimposition check: compare the mirror copy's substituent world positions to the original's after best-fit (Kabsch) alignment; color-match tolerance 0.25 units — flash matched spheres white and pulse mismatched ones (blue/yellow in CHXYZ) with a red outline. Labels (formulas, X/Y/Z/H, structural drawing) as CSS2DObject/HTML overlays anchored to world points so they stay crisp and screen-facing; the flat structural drawing can be a Line/ShapeGeometry group locked to face the camera. Toggle between rows cross-fades substituent colors in place rather than rebuilding the scene, reinforcing that only substituent variety changes.

authoredContext:
What causes molecular handedness? Look at generalized molecules of the type CH3X, CH2XY, and CHXYZ shown in the figure. On the left are three molecules, and on the right are their images reflected in a mirror. The CH3X and CH2XY molecules are identical to their mirror images and thus are not handed. If you make a molecular model of each molecule and its mirror image, you find that you can superimpose one on the other so that all atoms coincide. The CHXYZ molecule, by contrast, is not identical to its mirror image. You can’t superimpose a model of this molecule on a model of its mirror image for the same reason that you can’t superimpose a left hand on a right hand: they simply aren’t the same.

Tetrahedral carbon atoms and their mirror images. Molecules of the type CH3X and CH2XY are identical to their mirror images, but a molecule of the type CHXYZ is not. A CHXYZ molecule is related to its mirror image in the same way a right hand is related to a left hand.

The figure shows condensed formulas, structures, and ball-and-stick models of C H 3 X, C H 2 X Y, and C H X Y Z along with their mirror images.

A molecule that is not identical to its mirror image is a kind of stereoisomer (another section) called an enantiomer (e-nan-tee-oh-mer, from the Greek enantio, meaning “opposite”). Enantiomers are related to each other as a right hand is related to a left hand and result whenever a tetrahedral carbon is bonded to four different substituents (one need not be H). For example, lactic acid (2-hydroxypropanoic acid) exists as a pair of enantiomers because there are four different groups (−H, −OH, −CH3, −CO2H) bonded to the central carbon atom. The enantiomers are called (+)-lactic acid and (−)-lactic acid. Both are found in sour milk, but only the (+) enantiomer occurs in muscle tissue.

discrepancies: The source stacks all three compounds (CH3X, CH2XY, CHXYZ) as simultaneous rows sharing one tall mirror pane; the generated figure shows only one row at a time behind the compound toggle, so the side-by-side comparison that carries the source's message is lost at a glance.

In the source the reflected molecule appears to lie within/behind the glass pane (the pane covers all reflections); here the mirrored copy sits well to the right of the pane and only clips its edge, weakening the 'image in the mirror' reading.
The pane renders as an opaque grey slab rather than the pale blue translucent glass of the source (only the thin right edge is blue); the source's glassy tint and soft highlight are largely absent.

The 3D spheres in the source are noticeably larger/fuller relative to the short bonds (space-filling-ish ball-and-stick); here bonds are proportionally longer and thinner, making the models look sparser than the source.
The verdict text label, mismatch halos and emissive pulsing are additions not in the source figure (pedagogically useful but extra chrome).
evaluation.notes: A faithful and conceptually correct chirality figure with genuine 3D tetrahedral models, a correct 2D wedge drawing, and rich, meaningful interactions (row toggle, 4-step superimposition test, guided demo, draggable mirror copy), let down by the grey rather than glassy pane, the reflected copy sitting outside the pane, and small label sizing.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are correct (concept 5, no failure modes), but rendering details—opaque grey pane instead of translucent glass, mirrored copy positioned outside the pane, sphere/bond proportions, and small labels—are execution-level fixes for the generator.

Second column: flat 2D structural drawing — central black 'C', plain line up to X, plain lines down-left to H and down-right to H or Y, bold solid wedge down to H or Z
Third column: 3D ball-and-stick original model — dark gray carbon sphere at center
Red substituent sphere (X) bonded upward from carbon
Green substituent spheres (H) bonded to lower-left / lower-right / front
Blue substituent sphere (Y) replacing one green H in rows 2 and 3
Yellow substituent sphere (Z) replacing a second green H in row 3
Gray cylindrical bonds from carbon to each substituent (tetrahedral, 109.5°)
Tall pale-blue translucent rectangular mirror pane standing vertically at the right, with a diagonal white highlight streak and a darker blue edge line on its right side
Mirror-image ball-and-stick model behind/inside the pane, left-right reversed relative to the original, rendered slightly desaturated as if seen through glass
Faint specular reflection glints on spheres

interactions.teaches: Only the variety of substituents changes across rows; with four different groups on tetrahedral carbon the mirror image becomes non-superimposable
interactions.label: Compound

interactions.teaches: Dragging and spinning the reflected model onto the original shows CH3X and CH2XY can be brought into coincidence, while CHXYZ always leaves two colored substituents swapped
Seeing the tetrahedral arrangement from other angles proves the mismatch in CHXYZ is real 3D handedness, not an artifact of one viewpoint
The formal test for chirality: bring the mirror image out of the pane, attempt best-fit alignment, and read whether every sphere color matches
interactions.label: Superimposition test

demo_steps.title: CH3X in the mirror
demo_steps.narration: One red X and three identical green H's on a tetrahedral carbon; the pale pane shows the reflection with left and right substituents exchanged.

demo_steps.title: CH3X superimposes
demo_steps.narration: Pull the reflection out and rotate it onto the original: because the three green H's are interchangeable, every sphere matches. The molecule is achiral.

demo_steps.title: CH2XY still superimposes
demo_steps.narration: With red X, blue Y and two green H's, a simple rotation about the C–X bond still brings the mirror image into full coincidence — two identical groups are enough to kill handedness.

demo_steps.title: CHXYZ fails the test
demo_steps.narration: Four different groups: no matter how the reflection is rotated, the blue and yellow spheres end up swapped. The two forms are non-superimposable mirror images — the carbon is a chirality center.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World units: carbon sphere radius 0.42 at origin of the model; substituent spheres radius 0.38; bond cylinders radius 0.09, bond length 1.25 (center-to-center), perfect tetrahedral directions — X up at (0, 1.25, 0); the other three at 109.5° from it: lower-left (-1.02, -0.42, -0.35), lower-right (+1.02, -0.42, -0.35), front-down (0, -0.42, +1.10) which is the bold-wedge position pointing toward the viewer. Original model sits at x = 0; mirror plane is a vertical plane with normal along +X at x = +2.6, so the reflected copy is centered at x = +5.2 with all x-coordinates negated (left-right reversal). Mirror pane: 3.2 wide (along Z, receding) × 6.0 tall (Y) × 0.08 thick, standing vertically, its face nearly parallel to the screen and tilted ~8° so the highlight streak reads; pale blue #cfe3f0 at ~0.35 opacity, right edge line #4a8cb5, one diagonal white streak at ~60° from lower-left to upper-right at 0.5 opacity. Left of the models, on the same horizontal band: condensed formula text at x = -6.5 (C and H black #1a1a1a with H subscript green #00a14b in the source, X magenta #e5007e, Y blue #0077c8, Z gold #b8860b), and the flat 2D structural drawing centered at x = -3.4 drawn in the XY plane facing the camera (black 'C', thin black lines up/left/right, filled black triangular wedge pointing down-front, label letters colored as above, H labels green). Sphere colors: carbon #4a4a4a (dark gray, specular), X red #b0392b, H green #45a545, Y blue #2aa3dd, Z yellow #d6c92e; mirrored copy uses the same hues at ~80% saturation to suggest glass. Row identity only changes which of the three non-X positions carry green/blue/yellow: CH3X = green, green, green; CH2XY = green(lower-left), blue(lower-right), green(front-wedge); CHXYZ = green(lower-left), blue(lower-right), yellow(front-wedge). Whole scene spans about x ∈ [-7.5, 7], y ∈ [-3.2, 3.2].
interactionPlan.notes: Build one reusable molecule group (carbon + 4 substituents + bonds) and instantiate it twice; generate the mirror copy with scale(-1,1,1) on a parent group so it is a true reflection, then compensate geometry normals (THREE.Mesh material side = DoubleSide, or negate normals) to avoid inverted lighting. Mirror pane: MeshPhysicalMaterial, transmission ~0.6, roughness 0.15, transparent, depthWrite false, rendered last for correct blending; the streak is an additive plane or a canvas-texture gradient. Drag: raycast onto a plane parallel to the camera for translation; drag with modifier / horizontal drag beyond a threshold applies trackball rotation to the mirror copy only. Superimposition check: compare the mirror copy's substituent world positions to the original's after best-fit (Kabsch) alignment; color-match tolerance 0.25 units — flash matched spheres white and pulse mismatched ones (blue/yellow in CHXYZ) with a red outline. Labels (formulas, X/Y/Z/H, structural drawing) as CSS2DObject/HTML overlays anchored to world points so they stay crisp and screen-facing; the flat structural drawing can be a Line/ShapeGeometry group locked to face the camera. Toggle between rows cross-fades substituent colors in place rather than rebuilding the scene, reinforcing that only substituent variety changes.
